raw_text: His face was a chart of old sea-lanes, his squint a map of suns on foreign waters, his beard a tangle of briny frost, and his laugh a sudden squall that promised fair weather. Upon his hip he wore not a weapon, but a battered brass spyglass in a leather case, a tool he now used less for seeing far than for pointing things out that were near. "You've a look about you like a ship with a broken rudder," boomed the old sailor, clapping a hand upon the young man's shoulder. "Never," replied Arthur, his voice thin as the winter mist. "Have you never taken a turn about the docks with an old salt who knows the tides; meaning (for I am very old) the ones that pull on a man's own soul?" pursued the sailor. "I cannot say that I have," said Arthur. "I am afraid my walks have been solitary. Are there many such tides, Captain?" "More than all the herrings in the sea!" roared the man. "A fearsome school to swim against!" muttered Arthur. The old Captain, whom the whole port simply called 'The Captain', grinned. "Come, lad," said Arthur, with a newfound flicker of resolve, "take me where you please. I have been moored in my own gloom for a fortnight, and have learnt only the shape of my own sorrow. If there is a lesson in this fog, let me try to learn it." "Lay hold of my elbow!" Arthur did as he was told, and gripped the coarse wool of the Captain's coat. Instantly, the quiet sorrow, the empty room, the silent ticking of the clock, the very weight of his own stillness, all fell away. So did the genteel square in which he lived, and they stood upon the wharf on a Tuesday morning, where (for the tide was coming in) the city's heart beat a loud, percussive, and chaotic rhythm, in the unloading of the morning's catch from the fishing smacks. The hulls of the boats were black with tar and sea-stain, and their masts blacker, rising like a barren forest against the pearl-grey sheet of the sky, and against the dirtier grey of the harbour water; which last body had been churned up into a thick soup by the turning of screws and the dipping of oars; a soup that frothed and eddied in a hundred places where the mooring lines stretched taut; and made a filthy broth, thick with stray cabbage leaves and chips of wood. The air was heavy, and the nearest alleyways were choked with a sea-haze, half salt, half smoke, whose heavier portion clung to the granite setts in a slick and greasy film, as if all the fish in the Atlantic had, by some prior arrangement, rendered up their oil at once. There was little of beauty in the harbour or the weather, and yet there was an energy abroad that the most pristine country meadow on the clearest summer day could never hope to muster. For, the men who hauled the crates from the decks were roaring and full of purpose; calling out insults to one another from ship to shore, and now and then heaving a surplus mackerel--a far more honest missile than a whispered rumour--laughing uproariously if it struck its target and not one jot less if it missed and smote a post. The fishmongers' stalls were thrown open, and the merchants were glorious in their element. There were great, gleaming mounds of herring, their silver scales catching the dull light like a thousand dropped coins. There were solemn, whiskered cod, laid out on beds of ice like portly, sleeping aldermen, dreaming of their own corpulent importance. There were lobsters and crabs, piled high in wooden cages, waving their claws in slow, ponderous defiance, and clacking their shells with a sound like the winding of a hundred clocks. There were tubs of oysters, their rugged shells promising, in the fishmonger's benevolence, a pearl of a feast for a few pennies, that men's spirits might be restored gratis as they slurped them down; there were skeins of eels, dark and sinuous, recalling, in their writhing, ancient sea-serpents and the delightful terror of sailors' tales; there were great slices of salmon, pink and marbled, setting off the humble brown of the smoked kippers, and, in the sheer richness of their oily flesh, urgently demanding to be carried home in waxed paper and fried in butter for supper. The very gulls, set down among the offal and the discarded heads, though members of a greedy and squawking race, appeared to know that this was a special kind of chaos; and, to a bird, went strutting round and round their reeking world in a state of shrieking, passionate greed. The Coopers'! oh, the Coopers'! with their workshop doors wide open; and through that gap such industry! It was not alone that the hammers falling on the barrel staves made a deafening racket, or that the hot iron hoops hissed and steamed so angrily when fitted, or that the shavings curled up from the plane like wooden ribbons, or even that the blended scents of fresh-cut pine and hot metal were so bracing to the senses, or even that the finished barrels were so sturdy and round, the smaller kegs so neat, the great tuns so vast as to make the most ambitious brewer feel humbled and subsequently inspired. Nor was it that the apprentices were black with soot, or that the master cooper's hands were calloused and knowing, or that everything was useful and in its working dress; but the merchants were all so clamorous and so impatient for the day's delivery, that they argued over invoices at the doorway, counting on their fingers wildly, and forgot the tally on the wall, and came pushing back to check it, and committed a hundred similar blunders, in the best humour possible; while the Cooper and his men were so bluff and loud that the iron hoops with which they bound the staves might have been their own tempers, forged in the open for all to see, and for little boys to tap with sticks if they dared. But soon a factory whistle blew, calling good men all, to their midday meal, and away they shuffled, wiping their hands on their aprons. And at the same time there emerged from a dozen dockside taverns and cook-shops, innumerable women and children, carrying steaming pies and jugs of ale to their menfolk. The sight of these domestic commissaries appeared to interest the Captain very much, for he stood with Arthur beside him at a corner of the cooperage, and pointed with the brass end of his spyglass as they passed. And it was a very uncommon kind of gesture, for once or twice when a child stumbled and spilled a few drops of ale, he merely nodded wisely, and the father's good humour was not diminished in the slightest. For they said, it was a waste to fret over spilt drink on a working day. And so it was! God bless it, so it was! In time the whistle fell silent, and the hammering ceased; and yet there was a hearty promise of all these meals and the progress of their consumption, in the savoury steam that rose above each little family huddle; where the very air seemed to fatten as if it were dining too. "Is there a particular lesson in what you point at with your glass?" asked Arthur. "There is. My own." "Would it apply to any kind of work on this day?" asked Arthur. "To any honestly done. To a hard one most." "Why to a hard one most?" asked Arthur. "Because it needs it most." "Captain," said Arthur, after a moment's thought, "I wonder that you, of all the men in this great port, should desire to show me this toil and noise." "I!" cried the Captain. "You would have me believe that happiness is found in a day's hard labour, often for little pay, and with no guarantee of another," said Arthur. "Wouldn't you?" "I!" cried the Captain. "You seek to glorify this struggle on a Tuesday?" said Arthur. "And it amounts to the same thing." "I seek!" exclaimed the Captain. "Forgive me if I am wrong. I have heard it said in your name, or at least in that of your seafaring family," said Arthur. "There are some upon this earth of ours," returned the Captain, "who lay claim to know the sea, and who spin their yarns of romance, glory, freedom, and treasure in our name, who are as strange to us and all our kith and kin, as if they had never tasted salt. Remember that, and charge their fantasies to them, not us." Arthur promised that he would; and they went on, visible, as they had been all along, towards the heart of the city. It was a remarkable quality of the Captain (which Arthur had observed at the cooperage), that notwithstanding his rolling gait, he could navigate the most crowded lane with ease; and that he stood upon a muddy street corner quite as regally and like a master of his own world, as if he were on the quarter-deck of a great ship.

And yet there was no quarter-deck here, nor any wide expanse of sea, but only the ceaseless, churning tide of humanity that washed through the city's stone canyons. "Come," said the Captain, his voice a low rumble against the din, "the heart has chambers other than the counting-house; some darker, some with but a flickering light." Arthur, who had been contemplating the intricate patterns of mud and filth as a man might study a chart of unknown shoals, looked up and found the Captain's gaze fixed upon a narrow, uninviting alleyway. It was less a street than a crack in the city's grimy facade, a place into which the sun, even at its zenith, would fear to trespass. From its depths there issued a curious medley of odours: of boiling cabbage, of damp coal smoke, of wet wool, and underneath it all, the faint, persistent scent of decay, as if the very bricks were slowly surrendering to the river's damp embrace. "There?" asked Arthur, his revulsion thinly veiled by curiosity. "There," the Captain confirmed, and with a nod, he plunged into the gloom, leaving Arthur no choice but to follow in his wake. They had not taken ten paces before the roar of the main thoroughfare was muffled to a distant sigh, replaced by a more intimate and altogether more distressing chorus. The wail of an infant, sharp and demanding; the weary drone of a woman's voice, singing a lullaby with no joy in it; the sudden, angry clatter of a dropped pot from an upper window, followed by a torrent of invective that was blessedly indistinct. The alley was a living thing, its walls slick with moisture, its air thick with the exhalations of too many souls crowded into too little space. The Captain paused before a door that sagged upon its hinges, its paint peeled away by years of sorrow and neglect. He laid a hand upon the splintered wood, not to knock, but as if feeling for a pulse. "They cannot see us now," he murmured, "nor hear us. We are but shadows in their world, as they are often but figures in a ledger in yours." And as he spoke, the door and the wall around it became as transparent as grey-tinted glass, and Arthur found himself peering into a small, spare room. It was a meagre space, containing little more than a bed, a small table with two stools, a cold and empty hearth, and a single window that looked out upon a wall of blackened brick. A woman sat at the table, her back to them, her shoulders slumped in a posture of profound exhaustion. She was mending a child's small frock, her needle rising and falling in a slow, hypnotic rhythm, each stitch a tiny act of defiance against the encroaching poverty. A little girl, no more than five years of age, sat on the floor, her face pale and thin, listlessly arranging a small collection of shells into patterns on the grimy floorboards. A younger child, a mere babe, lay sleeping in a wooden crate that served as a cradle, its breath coming in shallow, wheezing gasps. "The wife of a second mate," the Captain said, his voice so low Arthur had to strain to hear it. "A good man, an able seaman. His ship, the 'Star of the East', is three months overdue from the Indies. His pay, and his life with it, are in the hands of the winds, the currents, and the underwriters at the Exchange." Arthur watched as the woman, whose name he knew must be Mary, or Anne, or some other common, gentle name, put down her sewing. She walked to the window and pressed her forehead against the cold glass, her gaze fixed on the sliver of cheerless sky visible between the rooftops. She did not weep; her sorrow seemed too deep, too old for such a simple release. She merely stood, a statue of anxious waiting. The little girl on the floor looked up at her mother's still form. "Is Da coming home for supper, Mama?" she asked, her voice small and clear as a little bell. The woman turned, and for a moment a light flickered in her weary eyes, a spark of maternal love that all the squalor of the room could not extinguish. She knelt and gathered the child into her arms. "Not for supper, my love," she said, her voice a soft croon. "But soon. He will come home soon, with silks for you and spices for the kitchen, and his pockets full of silver from the sea. Now, let us see if we can coax a little more life from the fire. There is a potato left for our dinner." She went to the hearth, and with a small, precious handful of coals, she began the laborious process of reviving the embers, her movements practiced and efficient. "You see?" whispered the Captain. "Honest toil, even in the waiting." "It is a grim sight," Arthur answered, his own throat feeling tight. "She has no guarantee. For all she knows, her husband lies in the deep, and she and her children are but a step away from the workhouse." "And whose name is on the charter-party of the 'Star of the East'?" the Captain asked, his question as sharp and pointed as a harpoon. "Whose firm stands to make a fortune if it arrives, and lose but a line in a ledger if it does not?" Arthur felt a flush of heat creep up his neck. He did not know the specific ship, but he knew the firm. He knew the partners. He had dined with them. He had heard them toast to favourable winds and rising premiums. "It is the way of business," he said, the words sounding hollow and foolish even to his own ears. "It is the way of the world," the Captain corrected him, "a world that men like you have built, plank by plank. A world where one man's fortune is another's long, anxious wait by a cold hearth. Come away. There is more to see." The grimy room dissolved, and they were once again in the clamour of the streets, but Arthur carried the image of the woman's face with him, a ghost more real than any phantom. The Captain led him onward, into the very heart of the city's commerce, to a building whose grand, columned facade seemed to sneer at the humble dwellings they had just left behind. This was the Merchant's Exchange. Oh, the Exchange! what a place it was! A great, echoing hall of marble and polished wood, with a domed ceiling so high it seemed to generate its own weather, a constant, low-hanging cloud of cigar smoke and self-importance. It was not a place of quiet contemplation, but a temple of tumult, a cathedral dedicated to the great god Mammon. And its worshippers were all so boisterous and so fervent in their devotions! There were great, stout men with watch-chains stretched tight across their expansive waistcoats, their faces florid with port and profit. They gathered in loud, gesticulating knots, their voices booming as they traded in the fates of unseen ships and unknown cargoes. Their laughter was a sudden, explosive bark, usually at the expense of a rival who had bought dear or sold cheap. There were lean, hawk-faced men, who darted through the crowds with ledgers tucked under their arms like holy texts, their eyes never still, always calculating, always searching for an angle, an advantage, a whisper of news that could be turned to gold. It was not alone that the staccato clatter of the telegraph machine made a frantic kind of music, or that the runners' feet slapped a brisk rhythm on the marble floor, or that the great board listing arrivals and departures was updated with a flourish like a conjuror's trick; but the very air hummed with a greedy energy. The blended scents of expensive leather, bay rum, and money, money, money, were so potent as to make an honest man feel light-headed and subsequently covetous. Nor was it that the columns were so massive, or that the brasswork was so highly polished, or that everything bespoke wealth and power; but the men themselves were so puffed up and so certain in the rightness of their world, that they bumped and jostled each other without apology, their eyes fixed on the middle distance of a balance sheet, and scribbled notes on their cuffs, and made and lost fortunes between one tick of the great clock and the next, in the best humour possible; while their clerks and junior partners hovered at the periphery, so eager and so imitative that the polished brass buttons on their coats might have been little gold coins, worn outside for general admiration, and for the senior partners to pluck at if they chose. Arthur knew this place. He knew the sound, the smell, the feeling of it. He saw men he knew, greeting them with a nod that was, of course, unseen. He saw Mr. Abernathy, of Abernathy, Watts, and Company, laughing heartily as he concluded a deal for a shipment of cotton, a deal that would render a hundred weavers in a northern town redundant. He saw old Lord Ashworth, who owned half the docks, conferring with his factor about raising the rents on the very tenements they had just visited. "The engine of the empire," Arthur murmured, half to himself, a phrase he had often used in speeches at his club. "An engine, to be sure," said the Captain, who stood beside him, solid and unimpressed as a granite bollard. "And what does this engine burn for fuel?" He pointed with the brass tip of his spyglass, a gesture that went entirely unnoticed in the hubbub. He did not point to the coal scuttles or the gas lamps. He pointed to Mr. Abernathy. "His fire is lit with the weaver's last shilling." He pointed to Lord Ashworth. "His boiler is stoked with the rents of the poor." He gestured to a jubilant young man who was accepting congratulations for a daring speculation on grain futures from the Americas. "And him. The 'Star of the East' is one of his ventures. See how he celebrates. The ship is not yet posted as lost, so to him, it is still an asset on a page, a potential for profit. The man, the second mate, his wife, his children; they are not even a footnote." "They take the risk!" Arthur protested, feeling a desperate need to defend this world, his world. "They risk their capital!" "Risk!" the Captain boomed, his voice for a moment cutting through the din like a foghorn, though only Arthur heard it. "They risk gold they have never touched. The sailor risks the breath in his lungs, the blood in his veins! They risk a number in a book. The sailor's wife risks her sanity, and his children risk their supper! Tell me, Arthur, which is the greater wager?" Arthur had no answer. The noise of the Exchange, which had once sounded to him like the vibrant pulse of prosperity, now seemed a shrill and manic cacophony, the senseless chatter of men gambling with stolen chips. The afternoon was waning, and a grey, weary light now filtered through the high, grimy windows of the Exchange as the last and most dogged of the merchants concluded their affairs. The Captain led Arthur out, away from the grand avenues of commerce and back into the labyrinth of humbler streets. The gas-lamps were being lit, casting long, dancing shadows and pools of uncertain yellow light. The mood of the city had changed. The brisk energy of the workday had given way to a tired shuffling, the sound of a thousand men and women trudging home to whatever comfort or misery awaited them. They walked for some time in silence, the Captain navigating the darkening streets with an unerring instinct, until they came to a place that Arthur had only ever heard of in whispers, a place spoken of as a final destination, a port of last resort. It was the Public Infirmary. A vast, grim block of a building, it seemed to absorb the light around it, its few lit windows glowing like malevolent eyes. The air here was different again; it was stagnant, heavy with the smell of carbolic acid, boiled laundry, and a deep, underlying note of human despair. "I have shown you the work," said the Captain, his voice low and solemn. "I have shown you the profit. Now, you must see the retirement." He did not need to make the walls transparent. He simply led Arthur through the main doors, their presence as unremarked as two motes of dust in a sunbeam. They entered a long, cavernous ward. Down either side were rows of narrow iron beds, so close together that a man might reach out and touch his neighbour's misery. In each bed lay a figure, some still, some stirring restlessly, some racked with coughs that echoed in the vaulted space like a morbid chorus. These were the old men. The broken men. The used-up men. Here was a man with hands gnarled into useless claws, his knuckles swollen to the size of walnuts; the hands of a rigger who had spent fifty years hauling on frozen ropes. Here was a man with a wheezing, ruined chest, his face the colour of old parchment; a ship's stoker who had breathed in a lifetime of coal dust. Here was another, his eyes wide and vacant, staring at a patch of damp on the ceiling, his mind lost somewhere in the South China Sea, muttering the names of tides and long-dead shipmates. "The final mooring," the Captain said, his voice a gravelly whisper. "After a life of honest, hard work. Here is where the engine discards its worn-out parts." Arthur felt a cold dread creep into his very bones, a chill that had nothing to do with the damp air of the ward. This was not a chart of commerce or a ledger of accounts; this was the raw, terrible truth of the matter. The Captain stopped beside a bed near the far end of the ward. The man in it was old, but it was a premature age, an age carved by hardship rather than time. His face was a mask of pain, his breathing a shallow, ragged struggle. He was alone. There was no wife, no child by his side. Only the institution's bleak, impersonal charity. "Look closely, Arthur," the Captain commanded. Arthur bent forward. There was something familiar in the high cheekbones, the set of the jaw, though it was all but lost in the skeletal ruin of the man's face. "Who is he?" Arthur asked. "His name is John. He was a cooper. A master of his trade," the Captain said. "He worked for more than thirty years at the same firm. A firm that built its fortune on the barrels he made, barrels that carried goods to every corner of the globe." The Captain paused, letting the silence stretch. "He worked for your grandfather, and for your father. He worked for you." Arthur recoiled as if struck. He stared at the dying man, and in the wreck of his features he tried to find the face of a man he must have seen a hundred times in the yards of his own family's business, a face he had never truly looked at, a name he had never bothered to learn. "I... I did not know," he stammered. "He was dismissed last year. His hands had begun to shake. He was no longer efficient." "Dismissed? But... but his pension! His service!" "The firm has no pension for labourers," the Captain stated, not as an accusation, but as a simple, damning fact. "It is not... economical." He used the word like a weapon, turning Arthur's own lexicon against him. Beneath the thin, coarse blanket, the Captain's hand moved, though Arthur could not be sure if he imagined it. He drew back the sheet, not from the man's body, but as if parting a great, heavy curtain from the very fabric of reality. And there, clinging to the dying man like a shroud, invisible to all but them, were two spectral figures. They were not children, but gaunt and terrible spectres of manhood. One was a hunched and twisted creature, its back bent from a lifetime of toil, its eyes hollow with a deep, bottomless Resignation. The other stood tall, but with a frightful, swaggering arrogance; its face was a mask of jaunty romance, its clothes a tattered, theatrical parody of a sailor's rig. It sang a silent sea-shanty, its mouth a black hole of empty bravado. "What are these?" Arthur cried, shrinking back. The light that had emanated from him, a steady, nautical glow, now flickered, and his voice sounded more distant, as if calling from the crow's nest in a gathering squall.

"My time is short," the Captain boomed, his form thinning, the room growing visible through his once-solid frame. "The tide recedes, and my voyage for this year is almost done. There is but one more thing you must see before I go."

He raised a translucent hand, and the scene of the family, of the humble room, did not vanish, but grew faint, like a memory. The sound of the woman's quiet weeping, which she had finally allowed herself now that her children were distracted, became a whisper on the wind. The Captain's face was now ancient, his skin like cracked parchment, his eyes like dying embers in the sockets of a skull. He loomed over Arthur, a colossus of fading power.

"You have seen the Reality of the life you decree for others," he rasped, the words echoing with the sound of a winter gale. "You have seen the false Romance you spin to hide the truth. But there is a consequence, Arthur, a final entry in the logbook, for those who sail your course."

He reached for Arthur, his hand no longer solid, but a cold mist that chilled Arthur to the bone. "I am the Spirit of this present time, born of this year's joy and this year's sorrow. The air was heavy with the smell of damp earth and decay. The Captain was now almost entirely transparent, a mere outline against the gloom, his great voice a final, fading echo.

"Beware the lie!" he thundered, his last ounce of strength seeming to go into the words. "Beware the jaunty tune that drowns the groans of dying men! For if the lie is not erased, the doom is sealed not only for them, but for you! For you!"

With a final, terrible groan, as of a great ship's timbers breaking apart upon a reef, the Captain dissolved into the mist. The spectral light was extinguished, and Arthur was plunged into a darkness so absolute, so profound, that it seemed to have a weight and a substance of its own. He was alone. Utterly, terrifyingly alone. He stood trembling, his heart a frantic drum against his ribs, the Captain's final warning ringing in his ears. He tried to call out, but his throat was tight with fear. He tried to move, but his feet were rooted to the spot.

And then, as his eyes struggled to adjust to the impenetrable blackness, he sensed he was no longer alone. There was no sound, no light, no touch. But a presence was there. It was a cold that did not come from the weather, a silence that was more than the absence of noise. Slowly, out of the deepest heart of the fog, a shape began to resolve itself. It was tall, and draped in a long, dark garment that seemed to be woven from the very fabric of the night itself. It moved towards him without a sound, a slow, inexorable drift, like a tide coming in. It had no face, no voice, no name that it would speak. It was a shadow, a dread, a final destination. And as it raised a single, bony hand, pointing forward into the gloom, Arthur knew, with a certainty that froze the very marrow in his bones, that his journey was not over, and that the greatest and most terrible lesson was yet to come. The bell began to toll, and it was not a ship's bell, but a funeral knell, and with each chime, Arthur felt his own world, the world he had built of gold and iron and indifference, begin to crumble into dust.

"A Merry Christmas to us all, my dears. God bless us!"

Which all the family re-echoed.

"Ha, ha!" laughed Scrooge's nephew. "Ha, ha, ha!"

She was very pretty: exceedingly pretty. The Phantom was shrouded in a deep black garment, which concealed its head, its face, its form, and left nothing of it visible save one outstretched hand. "I am in the presence of the Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come?" said Scrooge. The Spirit answered not, but pointed onward with its hand. "You are about to show me shadows of the things that have not happened, but will happen in the time before us," Scrooge pursued. "Is that so, Spirit?"

The upper portion of the garment was contracted for an instant in its folds, as if the Spirit had inclined its head. That was the only answer he received.

The Spirit paused a moment, as observing his condition, and giving him time to recover. But Scrooge was all the worse for this. "Ghost of the Future!" he exclaimed, "I fear you more than any spectre I have seen. But as I know your purpose is to do me good, and as I hope to live to be another man from what I was, I am prepared to bear you company, and do it with a thankful heart. Will you not speak to me?"

It gave him no reply. The hand was pointed straight before them.

"Lead on!" said Scrooge. "Lead on! The night is waning fast, and it is precious time to me, I know. Lead on, Spirit!"

The Phantom moved away as it had come towards him. Scrooge followed in the shadow of its dress, which bore him up, he thought, and carried him along.

They scarcely seemed to enter the city; for the city rather seemed to spring up about them, and encompass them of its own act. But there they were, in the heart of it; on 'Change, amongst the merchants; who hurried up and down, and chinked the money in their pockets, and conversed in groups, and looked at their watches, and trifled thoughtfully with their great gold seals; and so forth, as Scrooge had seen them often.

The Spirit stopped beside one little knot of business men. Observing that the hand was pointed to them, Scrooge advanced to listen to their talk.

"No," said a great fat man with a monstrous chin, "I don't know much about it, either way. I only know he's dead."

"When did he die?" inquired another.

"Last night, I believe."

"Why, what was the matter with him?" asked a third, taking a vast quantity of snuff out of a very large snuff-box. "I thought he'd never die."

"God knows," said the first, with a yawn.

"What has he done with his money?" asked a red-faced gentleman with a pendulous excrescence on the end of his nose, that shook like the gills of a turkey-cock.

"I haven't heard," said the man with the great chin, yawning again. "Left it to his company, perhaps. He hasn't left it to me. That's all I know."

This pleasantry was received with a general laugh.

"It's likely to be a very cheap funeral," said the same speaker; "for upon my life I don't know of anybody to go to it. Suppose we make up a party and volunteer?"

"I don't mind going if a lunch is provided," observed the gentleman with the excrescence on his nose. "But I must be fed, if I make one."

Another laugh.

"Well, I am the most disinterested among you, after all," said the first speaker, "for I never wear black gloves, and I never eat lunch. But I'll offer to go, if anybody else will. When I come to think of it, I'm not at all sure that I wasn't his most particular friend; for we used to stop and speak whenever we met. Bye, bye!"

Speakers and listeners strolled away, and mixed with other groups. Scrooge knew the men, and looked towards the Spirit for an explanation. The Phantom glided on into a street. Its finger pointed to two persons meeting. Scrooge listened again, thinking that the explanation might lie here.

He knew these men, also, perfectly. They were men of business: very wealthy, and of great importance. He had made a point always of standing well in their esteem: in a business point of view, that is; strictly in a business point of view.

"How are you?" said one.

"How are you?" returned the other.

"Well!" said the first. "Old Scratch has got his own at last, hey?"

"So I am told," returned the second. "Cold, isn't it?"

"Seasonable for Christmas time. You're not a skater, I suppose?"

"No. No. Something else to think of. Good morning!"

Not another word. That was their meeting, their conversation, and their parting.

Scrooge was at first inclined to be surprised that the Spirit should attach importance to conversations apparently so trivial; but feeling assured that they must have some hidden purpose, he set himself to consider what it was likely to be. They could scarcely be supposed to have any bearing on the death of Jacob, his old partner, for that was Past, and this Ghost's province was the Future. Nor could he think of any one immediately connected with himself, to whom he could apply them. But nothing doubting that to whomsoever they applied they had some latent moral for his own improvement, he resolved to treasure up every word he heard, and everything he saw; and especially to observe the shadow of himself when it appeared. For he had an expectation that the conduct of his future self would give him the clue he missed, and would render the solution of these riddles easy.

He looked about in that very place for his own image; but another man stood in his accustomed corner, and though the clock pointed to his usual time of day for being there, he saw no likeness of himself among the multitudes that poured in through the Porch. They left the busy scene, and went into an obscure part of the town, where Scrooge had never penetrated before, though he recognised its situation, and its bad repute. Alleys and archways, like so many cesspools, disgorged their offences of smell, and dirt, and life, upon the straggling streets; and the whole quarter reeked with crime, with filth, and misery.

Far in this den of infamous resort, there was a low-browed, beetling shop, below a pent-house roof, where iron, old rags, bottles, bones, and greasy offal, were bought. Upon the floor within, were piled up heaps of rusty keys, nails, chains, hinges, files, scales, weights, and refuse iron of all kinds. Secrets that few would like to scrutinise were bred and hidden in mountains of unseemly rags, masses of corrupted fat, and sepulchres of bones. Sitting in among the wares he dealt in, by a charcoal stove, made of old bricks, was a grey-haired rascal, nearly seventy years of age; who had screened himself from the cold air without, by a frowsy curtaining of miscellaneous tatters, hung upon a line; and smoked his pipe in all the luxury of calm retirement.

Ha, ha! We're all suitable to our calling, we're well matched. Come into the parlour. Come into the parlour."

"No, indeed," said Mrs. Dilber, laughing.

"It's the truest word that ever was spoke," said Mrs. Dilber. "It's a judgment on him."

"I wish it was a little heavier judgment," replied the woman; "and it should have been, you may depend upon it, if I could have laid my hands on anything else. Open that bundle, old Joe, and let me know the value of it. Speak out plain. I'm not afraid to be the first, nor afraid for them to see it. We knew pretty well that we were helping ourselves, before we met here, I believe. It's no sin. Open the bundle, Joe."

"That's your account," said Joe, "and I wouldn't give another sixpence, if I was to be boiled for not doing it. Who's next?"

Mrs. Dilber was next. Sheets and towels, a little wearing apparel, two old-fashioned silver teaspoons, a pair of sugar-tongs, and a few boots. Her account was stated on the wall in the same manner.

"Whose else's do you think?" replied the woman. "He isn't likely to take cold without 'em, I dare say."

They'd have wasted it, if it hadn't been for me."

"Putting it on him to be buried in, to be sure," replied the woman with a laugh. "Somebody was fool enough to do it, but I took it off again. The room was very dark, too dark to be observed with any accuracy, though Scrooge glanced round it in obedience to a secret impulse, anxious to know what kind of room it was. A pale light, rising in the outer air, fell straight upon the bed; and on it, plundered and bereft, unwatched, unwept, uncared for, was the body of this man.

The cover was so carelessly adjusted that the slightest raising of it, the motion of a finger upon Scrooge's part, would have disclosed the face. He thought of it, felt how easy it would be to do, and longed to do it; but had no more power to withdraw the veil than to dismiss the spectre at his side.

Oh cold, cold, rigid, dreadful Death, set up thine altar here, and dress it with such terrors as thou hast at thy command: for this is thy dominion! But of the loved, revered, and honoured head, thou canst not turn one hair to thy dread purposes, or make one feature odious. It is not that the hand is heavy and will fall down when released; it is not that the heart and pulse are still; but that the hand WAS open, generous, and true; the heart brave, warm, and tender; and the pulse a man's. Strike, Shadow, strike! And see his good deeds springing from the wound, to sow the world with life immortal!

But the Phantom, as ever, was unmoved. It neither stirred nor spoke, but kept its long, shadowy finger pointed with an unyielding finality at the shrouded head upon the bed. The gesture was more eloquent than any speech; it was a command, an indictment, and a prophecy all at once.

"I understand you," Scrooge returned, his voice trembling like a leaf in a gale. "And I would do your bidding if I could. But I have not the strength, Spirit. I have not the courage. Do not ask me to look upon that face."

He averted his eyes, squeezing them shut as if to blot out the very world, but the image of the bed was burned upon the inside of his lids. He knew, with a certainty that was colder and harder than any gravestone, whose features lay hidden by that wretched sheet. He knew, and the knowledge was an agony beyond all reckoning. Still, his cowardice clung to him like a second skin. He would not, could not, look.

The Phantom seemed to grow taller in the gloom, a pillar of impenetrable black. It raised its other hand, not in a threatening manner, but with a slow, deliberate grace that was somehow more terrible than any violence. It held the hand suspended in the air for a moment, and then, with an almost imperceptible flick of its phantasmal wrist, it gestured towards the bed.

A sudden, unnatural stillness fell upon the room. The motes of dust, which had danced in the pale, sickly light from the window, hung frozen in the air. A draft, which had been worrying a loose floorboard and making it creak like a coffin lid, was silenced. Then, with a slow, rustling sigh, like the exhalation of a dying man, the corner of the sheet covering the face began to lift. It rose, as if drawn by an invisible thread, folded back upon itself with a dreadful tidelessness, and settled.

And the face was revealed.

Scrooge did not scream. The sound was trapped in his throat, a hard, painful knot of pure terror. He saw the sharp, familiar features, now pinched and sharpened further by the hand of Death. The covetous eyes, forever closed; the thin, cruel lips, set in a final, eternal sneer of disapproval at the world; the lines of worry and avarice, now carved as deep as canyons in the cold, grey flesh. It was his own face. It was himself.

The breath he had been holding escaped him in a shuddering gasp. The room, the bed, the corpse of his own future self, all began to spin and dissolve into a vortex of swirling darkness. The pointing hand of the Spirit was the last thing he saw, a fixed point in a collapsing universe, and then that too was gone. He felt himself falling, tumbling through a cold and silent void, until his feet touched the ground once more.

He stood, not in the dark chamber of death, but in a small, humble room, bright with the light of a winter's day. But the light seemed to have no warmth in it; it was a cold, clinical glare that illuminated a scene of quiet, profound sorrow. He was in the Cratchit's house. But oh, how changed! The noisy cheerfulness that had once filled it to the rafters was gone, replaced by a hushed, oppressive stillness.

Mrs. Cratchit and her daughters were seated around the fire, their sewing laid in their laps. But their hands were idle, their needles still. They looked at the flames, but Scrooge could see they were not seeing them; their eyes were distant, fixed upon some inward, painful memory. Peter, looking older and graver than his years, sat in a corner with a book before him. But he did not turn the pages. He merely stared at the print, his brow furrowed in a frown that was not of concentration, but of grief.

"And he took a child, and set him in the midst of them," said Peter, his voice cracking on the last word, as he read aloud from the book. He could go no further. He closed the book with a quiet snap and buried his face in his hands.

His mother looked up, her own eyes brimming with tears. "The colour hurts my eyes," she said. She did not need to explain. The bit of sewing in her lap was black. "It makes them weak by candle-light; and I wouldn't show weak eyes to your father when he comes home, for the world. It must be near his time."

"Past it rather," Peter answered, looking up from his hands. "But I think he has walked a little slower than he used, these few last evenings, mother."

They were very quiet again. At last she said, and in a steady, cheerful voice, that only faltered once:

"I have known him walk with--I have known him walk with Tiny Tim upon his shoulder, very fast indeed."

"And so have I," cried Peter. "Often."

"And so have we all," cried all the others.

"But he was very light to carry," she resumed, her voice now trembling beyond her control, "and his father loved him so, that it was no trouble: no trouble. And there is your father at the door!"

She hurried out to meet her husband; a man as patient and as mild as ever, but Scrooge saw the lines of care etched deeper around his eyes, his shoulders stooped as if under a heavy, invisible burden. He came into the room with two of the younger children, who, upon seeing their mother, ran to her and were enfolded in her arms. Bob sat down in his accustomed chair, trying to smile, trying to be the cheerful patriarch his family needed him to be. But the effort was plain, and the smile was a fragile, heartbreaking thing.

"You went to-day, then, Robert?" said his wife.

"Yes, my dear," returned Bob. "I wish you could have gone. It would have done you good to see how green a place it is. But you'll see it often. I promised him that I would walk there on a Sunday. My little, little child!" cried Bob. "My little child!"

He broke down all at once. He couldn't help it. If he could have helped it, he and his child would have been farther apart perhaps than they were. He went into the little scullery, and after a moment, returned, his face washed and his composure somewhat regained. He sat with his family, and they spoke of Tiny Tim; of his gentleness, his patience, his ever-present kindness. They recalled his little sayings, the funny way he had of looking at the world, the pure, untainted goodness that had shone from him like a light.

Scrooge watched, a silent, invisible witness to their grief. A grief he now understood he had authored. He saw the empty stool by the fireplace, the little crutch, carefully preserved, resting in a corner. Each object was a dagger in his heart.

"Spirit," he whispered, his voice hoarse with unshed tears. "Something tells me that our parting moment is at hand. I know it, but I know not how. Tell me what man that was whom we saw lying dead?"

The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come, as before, made no reply. It merely turned, its dark robes flowing behind it like the waters of a black river, and beckoned him to follow.

The quiet sorrow of the Cratchit home dissolved, and they were standing once more in the bustling heart of the city. But it was not the festive, snow-covered city he had seen with the Ghost of Christmas Present. This was a city of grim commerce, of hurried footsteps and anxious faces. They stood before the Exchange, and Scrooge saw a group of his old business associates gathered on the steps, their conversation punctuated by the chinking of coins in their pockets.

"Well," said a great fat man with a monstrous chin, "I don't know much about it, either way. I only know he's dead."

"When did he die?" inquired another.

"Last night, I believe."

"Why, what was the matter with him?" asked a third, taking a vast quantity of snuff out of a large snuff-box. "I thought he'd never die."

"God knows," said the first, with a yawn.

"What has he done with his money?" asked a red-faced gentleman with a pendulous excrescence on the end of his nose, that shook like the gills of a turkey-cock.

"I haven't heard," said the man with the large chin, yawning again. "Left it to his company, perhaps. He hasn't left it to me. That's all I know."

This pleasantry was received with a general laugh.

"It's likely to be a very cheap funeral," said the same speaker; "for upon my life I don't know of anybody to go to it. Suppose we make up a party and volunteer?"

"I don't mind going if a lunch is provided," observed the gentleman with the excrescence on his nose. "But I must be fed, if I make one."

Another laugh. The group dispersed, their minds already turning to matters of profit and loss, the dead man utterly forgotten, a mere footnote in the day's ledger.

Scrooge looked at the Phantom, his heart a cold, heavy stone in his chest. "Spirit!" he implored. "I see now that this man's death brought no sorrow, no compassion, not even a moment's genuine reflection. His life was a lonely pursuit of gain, and his death is but a piece of news, to be traded and forgotten. Let me see some tenderness connected with a death, or that dark chamber, Spirit, which we left just now, will be forever present to me."

The Phantom glided onward, leading him away from the clatter of commerce and into the winding, narrow streets of the city's poorer quarters. The scene shifted again, and they were in a different place, a place Scrooge knew with a dreadful familiarity. It was his own counting-house.

But how different it was! The sign above the door, 'Scrooge and Marley,' had been painted over, and a new, more ostentatious one had been erected in its place: 'Dobson, Fipps, and Company. Financial Agents.' The very air of the place seemed changed. The musty, miserly chill was gone, replaced by a bustling, if somewhat ruthless, energy. Inside, two young men with sharp, calculating eyes sat at desks where Scrooge and Bob Cratchit had once laboured. The room was warmer, better lit, and yet it felt colder to Scrooge than his own icy chamber ever had.

"A fine piece of business, Fipps, acquiring the old man's ledgers," said the one named Dobson, a man with a smile that did not reach his eyes. "There are debts here he let fester for years. With a bit of modern pressure, we'll squeeze them dry in a month."

"He was a fool," replied Fipps, not looking up from the book he was scrutinising. "He had the iron fist, but not the wit to use it properly. Content to hoard his little pile, when he could have been building an empire. His passing is the best thing that could have happened to this firm."

"Did you hear about the funeral?" asked Dobson, with a smirk. "Cratchit, his old clerk, was the only one there. Stood by the hole in the ground all by himself. A loyalty the old skinflint certainly never earned."

"More fool him," muttered Fipps. "Wasting a working day on sentiment. It's a wonder we kept him on, Dobson."

"Charity, my dear Fipps," said Dobson, laughing a dry, rasping laugh. "A little charity. It looks good in the annual report. Now, about that mortgage on the baker's shop..."

Scrooge could bear no more. He turned to the Spirit, his whole body shaking with a mixture of rage, shame, and abject terror. This was his legacy. To be a joke to his peers, a cautionary tale of foolishness to his successors, a memory of cold neglect to the only man who showed him a scrap of loyalty.

He staggered back from the window, and found himself in a place he had not yet seen. The air was thick with damp and decay. It was a churchyard. A wretched, overgrown, and neglected place, choked with weeds and long, coarse grass. It was a place for the forgotten, the unloved, the paupers whose lives and deaths had made no mark upon the world. The Spirit stood among the graves, and pointed to one.

Scrooge advanced towards it, trembling. He crept towards the grave, following the pointing finger, his feet dragging as if weighted with lead. He knew, he knew what he would find. But still he had to see. The Spirit stood, as it had before the shrouded corpse, its finger unwavering, its silence more damning than any accusation.

"Before I draw nearer to that stone to which you point," said Scrooge, "answer me one question. Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of things that May be, only?"

Still the Ghost pointed downward to the grave by which it stood.

"Men's courses will foreshadow certain ends, to which, if persevered in, they must lead," said Scrooge. "But if the courses be departed from, the ends will change. Say it is so with what you show me!"

The Spirit was immovable as ever.

Scrooge crept towards it, trembling as he went; and following the finger, read upon the stone of the neglected grave his own name, EBENEZER SCROOGE.

"Am I that man who lay upon the bed?" he cried, upon his knees.

The finger pointed from the grave to him, and back again.

"No, Spirit! Oh no, no!"

The finger still was there.

"Spirit!" he cried, clutching at its robe, his voice a ragged plea. "Hear me! I am not the man I was. I will not be the man I must have been but for this intercourse. Why show me this, if I am past all hope?"

For the first time the hand appeared to shake. There was a B in its touch, a sympathy that Scrooge had not felt before.

"Good Spirit," he pursued, as down upon the ground he fell before it, "Your nature intercedes for me, and pities me. Assure me that I may yet change these shadows you have shown me, by an altered life!"

The kind hand trembled.

"I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future. The Spirits of all Three shall strive within me. I will not shut out the lessons that they teach. Oh, tell me I may sponge away the writing on this stone!"

In his agony, he caught the spectral hand. It sought to free itself, but he was strong in his entreaty, and detained it. The Spirit, stronger yet, repulsed him.

Holding up his hands in a last prayer to have his fate reversed, he saw an alteration in the Phantom's hood and dress. It shrunk, collapsed, and dwindled down into a bedpost.
